papers.title: CZ CELLxGENE Discover: a single-cell data platform for scalable exploration, analysis and modeling of aggregated data
papers.reason: Labeled data platform using Cell Ontology IDs
papers.why_listed: Standardized labeled data with Cell Ontology IDs

sources.label: Europe PMC full text (results, methods, data availability)

ingestion.notes: Platform paper; methods describe the Gene Expression pipeline as of October 2023. Corpus size (93M+ cells) will have grown since.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: CZ CELLxGENE Discover hosts over 93 million standardized single cells with consistent, ontology-based metadata, and offers tools to explore single datasets, compare gene expression across the corpus, see computed marker genes per cell type, and stream data for analysis or model training.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Single-cell data is scattered across portals with inconsistent metadata, which blocks cross-study meta-analysis and training of large models.

sections.heading: Standardized schema
sections.body: Every submitted dataset must meet a minimal, versioned schema of 11 required fields (cell type, tissue, disease, assay, ancestry, etc.) using ontologies such as the Cell Ontology and UBERON, and must include raw counts and at least one 2D embedding. CELLxGENE doesn't re-cluster or re-annotate submissions.

sections.heading: Corpus
sections.body: 93M+ unique cells across 449 tissues and 40 assay types; 63% human and 32% mouse. About 62% of human data is from healthy donors and 38% spans 132 diseases. Ethnic diversity and age groups are underrepresented.

sections.heading: Tools
sections.body: Explorer visualizes single datasets of up to ~4.3M cells interactively, with differential expression. Gene Expression averages normalized expression per cell type and tissue across datasets, using the Cell Ontology to roll child types up into parents, and lists 25 computed marker genes per cell type. Census gives Python/R access to the whole corpus through TileDB-SOMA, including out-of-core statistics and PyTorch data loaders.

sections.heading: Validation
sections.body: ANOVA found no significant dataset or assay differences in averaged expression for most tested cell types, suggesting aggregation plus log normalization partly reduces batch effects. Computed marker genes recalled 33% of HuBMAP canonical markers across 127 cell types.

key_findings: Largest standardized single-cell corpus, labeled with Cell Ontology terms
Per-cell-type marker genes from a bootstrapped Welch's t-test effect size
Cell Ontology roll-up handles datasets labeled at different granularity
limitations: Cell type labels come from submitters; CELLxGENE doesn't re-annotate them
Batch effects are only partly reduced; rare cell types remain affected
Computed markers recall only about a third of HuBMAP canonical markers
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (labeled data resource, preferred). The reference that CellTypeAgent uses to verify LLM proposals, and a large source of Cell Ontology–labeled immune and tumor data for benchmarking our agent. Its expression summaries are a way for an agent to check a proposed label against real data.

sequencing.summary: Hosts data from 40 transcriptomic assays; only assays without gene-length normalization enter Gene Expression.

quantification.summary: Raw count matrices are required at submission so data can be reused without realignment.

preprocessing.summary: Gene Expression pipeline: drop duplicate cells and cells with <500 genes, normalize to ln(CPTT + 1), mask very low values; marker genes by Welch's t-test with bootstrapped effect sizes. Census adds out-of-core mean, variance and highly variable gene calculations.

dimensionality_reduction.summary: Submitters must supply at least one 2D embedding (UMAP, t-SNE or PCA) for display.

batch_correction.summary: No integration is applied; the paper tests how far averaging and log normalization alone reduce batch effects (repeated-measures ANOVA).

annotation.summary: Standardizes submitters' cell type labels to Cell Ontology terms, rolls expression up the ontology, and publishes computed marker genes per cell type and tissue, making it a reference for annotation and its verification.

algorithms.name: Welch's t-test marker genes
algorithms.description: 10th percentile of effect sizes across pairwise cell type comparisons, bootstrapped; top 25 genes.

papers.title: CellMarker 2.0: an updated database of manually curated cell markers in human/mouse and web tools based on scRNA-seq data
papers.reason: Curated marker database; direct source of marker rules
papers.why_listed: Largest manually curated marker database; direct source of rules

ingestion.notes: Database paper; no benchmark. The database URL is taken from the paper; on 2026-11-10 it returned HTTP 403 to an automated check (may block scripts) and the IP mirror didn't respond.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: CellMarker 2.0 is a manually curated database of experimentally supported cell-type markers for human and mouse (26,915 markers, 2,578 cell types, 656 tissues, 83,361 tissue–cell type–marker entries), with web tools for annotating, clustering and analyzing scRNA-seq data.

sections.heading: What's in it
sections.body: Curated from 24,591 papers (mostly 2019–2022, journals with impact factor >7), adding 36,300 entries to version 1.0. Each entry records species, tissue (Uberon ID), cell type (Cell Ontology ID), marker gene identifiers, marker type (26 gene types including protein-coding genes and lncRNAs), sequencing technology (48, e.g. 10x Chromium, Smart-seq2, Drop-seq) and the source publication. It covers 355 cancer types' cell markers.

sections.heading: Web tools
sections.body: Six modules run on 108 bundled human disease datasets (38 diseases, 1.47 million cells): cell annotation from a list of differentially expressed genes, clustering with UMAP/t-SNE (Seurat), malignancy via copy number (InferCNV), differentiation trajectories (Monocle 3), feature gene expression, and cell–cell communication (CellPhoneDB).

sections.heading: Access
sections.body: Searchable by tissue, cell type or marker, browsable by category, and fully downloadable.

key_findings: Largest manually curated human/mouse marker resource, with ontology IDs for tissues and cell types
Markers are tagged by sequencing technology and gene type, which can help filter for scRNA-seq-relevant markers
Includes tumor-cell markers across hundreds of cancer types
limitations: Curation was limited to journals with impact factor above 7
No benchmark of the annotation tool's accuracy in this paper
Human and mouse only
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 4 (curated marker source, preferred). The most direct source of raw marker rules for the project, with ontology IDs that let our agent standardize labels. Several ingested methods (ScType, CASSIA's RAG agent, GPTCelltype's benchmark) already build on it.

sequencing.summary: Markers are annotated with the sequencing technology they came from (48 technologies).

preprocessing.summary: Web tool computes differentially expressed genes between clusters.

dimensionality_reduction.summary: Web tool offers UMAP and t-SNE.

clustering.summary: Web tool clusters bundled datasets at user-chosen resolution.

annotation.summary: Curated tissue–cell type–marker database with ontology IDs; a web tool scores cell types from a user's differentially expressed genes, and all modules label cells from the database.

trajectory.summary: Web tool runs differentiation and gene trajectories.

cell_communication.summary: Web tool runs ligand–receptor interaction analysis.

papers.title: Zero-shot evaluation reveals limitations of single-cell foundation models
papers.reason: Evaluation of foundation models for annotation; documents their gaps

sources.label: Europe PMC full text (results, conclusions, methods, data and code availability)

ingestion.notes: Numeric scores are in supplementary tables, which weren't read; results are described as the text states them.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: Used without fine-tuning, the single-cell foundation models scGPT and Geneformer separate cell types and remove batch effects worse than simple baselines: selecting highly variable genes, scVI or Harmony.

sections.heading: Question
sections.body: Foundation models are usually judged after fine-tuning on labeled data. In discovery settings there are no labels, so their embeddings must work zero-shot. Do they?

sections.heading: Setup
sections.body: Cell embeddings from Geneformer and three scGPT variants (pretrained on kidney, blood or 33M human cells) versus baselines: 2,000 highly variable genes (HVG), scVI and Harmony, the last two trained on each dataset. Five human datasets: pancreas (five sources), PBMC 12k, PBMC 95k, a cross-tissue immune atlas and Tabula Sapiens. Metrics from the scIB benchmark: AvgBIO (mean of silhouette, NMI and ARI on Louvain clusters) for cell type separation; batch silhouette and principal component regression for batch mixing.

sections.heading: Cell type separation
sections.body: Both foundation models scored below HVG, scVI and Harmony on AvgBIO in general; scGPT beat the baselines only on PBMC 12k. Pretraining helped scGPT over a random-weight model, but the 33M-cell model didn't beat the blood-only model. Doing well didn't track whether a dataset had been seen in pretraining.

sections.heading: Batch integration
sections.body: Geneformer ranked last on nearly every batch metric, with embeddings dominated by batch. scGPT corrected batches within a technology but not across technologies. scVI and Harmony handled technical batches better; scGPT did better only on Tabula Sapiens and the immune atlas, both in its pretraining data. Raw HVG gave the best full-dimension batch scores.

sections.heading: Why
sections.body: Both models struggle with their own pretraining task: scGPT's expression predictions barely beat predicting the mean, and Geneformer's gene rankings correlate only moderately with the truth (median r = 0.56). The authors question whether masked-language-model pretraining yields useful cell embeddings.

key_findings: Zero-shot scGPT and Geneformer don't consistently beat HVG, scVI or Harmony
More pretraining data didn't always help
Evaluation is confounded when benchmark datasets were part of pretraining; the authors call for held-out benchmark datasets
limitations: Only two foundation models and five datasets; transcriptomic data only
Some evaluation datasets overlap with pretraining data
Doesn't test fine-tuned performance
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (benchmark, preferred). A warning for our agent design: foundation-model embeddings can't be assumed to help annotation without fine-tuning, and simple baselines (HVG, scVI, Harmony) should always be in our benchmarks. It also models the benchmark hygiene we need: keep evaluation data out of anything a model has seen.

preprocessing.summary: 2,000 highly variable genes as a baseline representation; model-specific input encoding (Geneformer gene ranks, scGPT 50 expression bins).

dimensionality_reduction.summary: The paper compares cell embeddings (latent spaces) from foundation models with HVG, scVI and Harmony for separating cell types.

batch_correction.summary: Zero-shot batch integration of foundation models versus Harmony and scVI, scored with batch silhouette and principal component regression.

clustering.summary: Louvain clustering across 20 resolutions on each embedding, scored with NMI and ARI against known labels.

annotation.summary: Motivated by annotation in label-free settings; evaluates whether embeddings separate known cell types, not label assignment itself.

algorithms.name: scGPT
algorithms.description: Transformer pretrained with masked expression-bin prediction; 12 layers.

algorithms.name: Geneformer
algorithms.description: BERT-style transformer on gene rank order; 6 layers.

papers.title: Integrated analysis of multimodal single-cell data
papers.reason: Seurat v4/Azimuth reference mapping with a protein-validated PBMC reference
papers.why_listed: Seurat v4 / Azimuth; CITE-seq PBMC reference with protein-validated labels

sources.label: Europe PMC full text (results, discussion, STAR Methods)

ingestion.notes: Vaccination-response and multi-modality benchmark sections were skimmed. Level 3 marker lists are in Figure S4 and weren't read; markers below are those named in the text (several are surface proteins measured by CITE-seq).

enhanced_abstract.tldr: Seurat v4 introduces weighted-nearest-neighbor (WNN) analysis to combine RNA with surface protein (or other modalities) per cell, uses it to build a 211,000-cell CITE-seq reference of human PBMCs annotated at three levels (8/30/57 types), and maps new RNA-only datasets onto it, the basis of the Azimuth web app.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: RNA and protein each separate some cell types better than the other: CD4 vs. CD8 T cells blur in RNA but split cleanly by protein, while dendritic cells are clear in RNA but not with a limited antibody panel. Analysis needs to learn, per cell, which modality to trust.

sections.heading: WNN method
sections.body: Build a k-nearest-neighbor graph per modality, predict each cell's profile from its neighbors in each modality, turn the prediction accuracy into per-cell modality weights (summing to 1), then build one combined neighbor graph from the weighted similarities. That graph feeds UMAP, clustering and trajectory analysis.

sections.heading: PBMC reference
sections.body: CITE-seq of 210,911 PBMCs from eight vaccine-trial volunteers at three timepoints, with up to 228 antibodies. Samples integrated with Seurat anchors (SCTransform + reciprocal PCA), then WNN clustering found 57 clusters, grouped into 30 and 8 broader labels, including very rare AXL+ SIGLEC6+ dendritic cells and new lymphoid subsets validated by flow cytometry.

sections.heading: Reference mapping
sections.body: Supervised PCA learns the transcriptome directions that best reproduce the WNN structure. Query scRNA-seq data are projected into that space, matched with anchors (mutual nearest neighbors), and labeled by anchor-weighted voting, then placed on the reference UMAP. Applied to COVID-19 PBMCs, it split T cells into 12 groups versus 6 in the original study and found MAIT cell depletion, confirmed by CyTOF.

sections.heading: Benchmark
sections.body: Against scArches on a held-out CITE-seq query, the two agreed on 67% of cells; where they disagreed, the held-out protein data supported Seurat's label 79% of the time.

key_findings: Combining modalities resolves immune states that RNA or protein alone blur together
A protein-validated, three-level PBMC reference that RNA-only data can be mapped onto in minutes (Azimuth)
Cells absent from the reference (e.g. neutrophils in COVID-19) can't be mapped and land on cluster borders
limitations: PBMC reference only: few granulocytes or erythrocytes, and no tumor tissue
WNN assumes the modalities don't define conflicting cell states
Reference mapping can only assign labels present in the reference
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (algorithm and labeled reference, preferred). Seurat is the most-used toolkit across the ingested papers, and its Azimuth PBMC reference gives protein-validated immune labels, a strong ground truth for testing our agent on monocytes and T cell subsets.

sequencing.summary: CITE-seq on 10x Chromium 3′ (228 antibodies) and ECCITE-seq on 10x 5′ (54 antibodies, with TCR), sequenced on NovaSeq.

quantification.summary: RNA aligned to GRCh38 with Cell Ranger 3.1.0; antibody and hashtag counts with Alevin.

preprocessing.summary: Removed cells with <500 or >6,000 genes or excessive antibody counts; doublets by HTODemux plus a neighbor-based within-sample doublet filter; SCTransform for RNA and CLR normalization for protein.

dimensionality_reduction.summary: PCA per modality (40 RNA / 50 protein dims) feeds WNN; supervised PCA defines the reference space for mapping; queries projected onto the reference UMAP.

batch_correction.summary: Anchor-based integration with SCTransform and reciprocal PCA across 24 samples, with day-0 samples as reference; anchors also align queries to the reference.

clustering.summary: Shared-nearest-neighbor graph from the WNN graph, clustered with the SLM algorithm at high resolution, then clusters merged by differential expression and rare types sub-clustered.

annotation.summary: Three-level manual annotation of the reference from RNA and protein markers; queries labeled by anchor-weighted voting after supervised-PCA projection (Azimuth). Benchmarked against scArches.

trajectory.summary: WNN graph can feed trajectory inference; continuous naive-to-memory B cell and NK cell gradients described.

algorithms.name: Weighted nearest neighbor (WNN)
algorithms.description: Per-cell modality weights from cross-modality neighbor predictions, combined into one neighbor graph.

algorithms.name: Supervised PCA
algorithms.description: Projection that best captures the WNN structure, used for mapping RNA-only queries.

papers.title: Cross-tissue immune cell analysis reveals tissue-specific features in humans
papers.reason: CellTypist: immune annotation models plus a curated immune cell encyclopedia
papers.why_listed: CellTypist: immune-focused logistic regression models + curated immune encyclopedia

ingestion.notes: CellTypist model details are in the Supplementary Text, which wasn't read. Marker genes below are those named in the main text.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: A 360,000-cell scRNA-seq + VDJ atlas of immune cells from 16 tissues of 12 organ donors, annotated with CellTypist, a fast logistic-regression classifier trained on harmonized immune labels from 20 tissues that now covers 101 immune cell types.

sections.heading: Goal
sections.body: Map immune cell types across human tissues (not just blood) at fine resolution, and build an automated, updatable way to annotate immune cells consistently across datasets.

sections.heading: CellTypist
sections.body: Immune cells from 19 published datasets across 20 tissues were given harmonized labels at two levels: 32 broad types and 91 fine types. L2-regularized logistic regression trained with stochastic gradient descent in mini-batches, then retrained on the union of the top 300 genes per cell type. Precision, recall and F1 were around 0.9 at both levels, and it held up against sparse data and batch effects. Cell types with more training cells were predicted more accurately.

sections.heading: Atlas
sections.body: 16 tissues from 12 deceased donors, including bone marrow, spleen, lymph nodes, blood, gut, lung and liver; 357,211 cells passed QC. CellTypist plus manual curation resolved 43 cell states, with T and B cell receptor sequencing tracking clones across tissues. The 41 cell types found were fed back into CellTypist, which now has 101 annotated types.

sections.heading: Myeloid findings
sections.body: Separated monocytes from macrophages, which often blur together in scRNA-seq. Classical and non-classical monocytes differed in CD14, FCGR3A and CX3CR1. Macrophages were strongly tissue-specific (alveolar, erythrophagocytic, intestinal), and three DC subsets were resolved (DC1, DC2, migratory DCs).

sections.heading: T cell findings
sections.body: Separated naive/central-memory, Tfh, Treg, effector-memory and tissue-resident Th1/Th17 CD4 T cells; three memory CD8 subsets (gut-resident, effector-memory/TEMRA, Trm/em); MAIT cells; two γδ populations; NK and ILC3. Expanded clones were mostly tissue-resident memory cells, and the largest clones spread across five or more tissues.

key_findings: A pretrained, organ-agnostic immune classifier with ~0.9 F1 at both broad and fine levels
The reference can be updated: new curated types are fed back into the model
Many immune subsets are tissue-restricted, so a blood-only reference misses them
Main text gives explicit marker sets for monocyte, DC and T cell subsets
limitations: Healthy organ donors only; no tumor tissue
Accuracy is lower for cell types with few training cells
Fine subtypes still needed manual curation on top of automatic labels
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (algorithm, preferred) and a marker source (rule 4). CellTypist is a strong reference-based baseline for immune annotation, and this paper gives explicit markers for the group's two focus lineages, monocytes and T cells. It covers healthy tissue rather than cancer, so tumor-specific states need other sources.

sequencing.summary: 10x Genomics Chromium 5′ (v1/v2) and 3′ (v3) scRNA-seq plus paired TCRαβ, TCRγδ and BCR libraries; HiSeq 4000 / NovaSeq 6000.

quantification.summary: Alignment and counting with Cell Ranger 6.1.1; VDJ with cellranger-vdj and a custom γδ pipeline (dandelion).

preprocessing.summary: Removed cells with <1,000 UMIs and <600 genes; doublets with Scrublet; hashtag demultiplexing with Hashsolo; normalization in Scanpy.

dimensionality_reduction.summary: Standard Scanpy workflow (details in the supplement).

batch_correction.summary: Integration with BBKNN and scVI, compared with kBET; CellTypist itself was robust to batch effects.

clustering.summary: Graph-based clustering in Scanpy, followed by manual sub-clustering of compartments.

annotation.summary: CellTypist logistic-regression models at broad (32 types) and fine (91 types) levels, then manual curation with known markers and cross-validation in independent datasets; curated types fed back to update the model.

cell_communication.summary: Not addressed (TCR clonal sharing across tissues is analyzed instead).

algorithms.name: CellTypist logistic regression
algorithms.description: L2-regularized, trained by stochastic gradient descent on harmonized immune labels.

papers.title: TISCH2: expanded datasets and new tools for single-cell transcriptome analyses of the tumor microenvironment
papers.reason: Uniformly annotated tumor microenvironment datasets

ingestion.notes: The processing pipeline (MAESTRO) is cited rather than described, so the specific QC, batch, clustering and annotation methods are not named in this paper.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: TISCH2 is a web resource of 190 uniformly processed and annotated tumor scRNA-seq datasets (~6.3 million cells, 50 cancer types, human and mouse), now with cell–cell communication, transcription factor, survival and gene-correlation analyses.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: A tumor microenvironment single-cell portal. Datasets are found by text-mining GEO and ArrayExpress, curated by hand with sample metadata, then all processed through the same MAESTRO workflow: QC, batch removal, clustering, differential expression, cell type annotation, malignant cell classification and gene set enrichment.

sections.heading: Scale
sections.body: ~6.3M cells from 190 datasets across 50 cancer types and 20 tissues (about triple the first TISCH). 40 datasets include treatment conditions such as immunotherapy, chemotherapy and targeted therapy; immunotherapy datasets get extra responder-vs-nonresponder comparisons.

sections.heading: New analyses
sections.body: Cell–cell communication per dataset with CellChat (significant ligand–receptor pairs between cell types); transcription factor enrichment per cluster with LISA; survival hazard ratios across 33 TCGA cancer types; and gene–gene correlation computed on mini-clusters of 30 similar cells to reduce dropout noise.

sections.heading: Example
sections.body: SPI1 and STAT1 came out as top regulators of a monocyte/macrophage cluster in head and neck cancer, and that cluster was predicted to suppress CD8 T cells via CD80–CTLA4.

key_findings: Uniformly annotated tumor datasets make cross-study comparison of immune cell types possible
Includes treatment and immunotherapy-response datasets
All matrices, annotations, DEGs and interaction results are downloadable
limitations: Cell type labels come from an automated pipeline; their accuracy isn't benchmarked in this paper
Methods details are deferred to MAESTRO and the first TISCH paper
No trajectory analysis yet (planned)
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (labeled tumor data resource, preferred). A large, cancer-specific source of annotated immune and tumor cells for benchmarking our agent in the setting the group cares about, including monocytes/macrophages and CD8 T cells. Its labels are automated, so they should be checked before being treated as ground truth.

preprocessing.summary: Uniform QC and differential expression via the MAESTRO workflow; gene correlations on averaged mini-clusters of 30 cells.

batch_correction.summary: Batch effects between samples removed within MAESTRO; method not named here.

clustering.summary: Cell clustering within MAESTRO; method not named here.

annotation.summary: Uniform cell type annotation and malignant cell classification via MAESTRO, producing consistently labeled TME datasets.

cell_communication.summary: CellChat run per dataset with standard parameters; significant ligand–receptor pairs (p < 0.05) and communication probabilities shown per cell type.

algorithms.description: Transcription factor enrichment from chromatin and ChIP-seq models.

papers.title: Assessing GPT-4 for cell type annotation in single-cell RNA-seq analysis
papers.reason: GPT-4 annotation from marker lists, benchmarked against manual labels
papers.why_listed: GPTCelltype: LLM annotation from marker lists; benchmarked vs manual

sources.label: Europe PMC full text (main text, Methods, data availability)

ingestion.notes: Figures and supplementary tables were not available in the text; results are described from the main text.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: GPT-4, given a cluster's top marker or differential genes, names the cell type in close agreement with expert labels, and beats SingleR, ScType and CellMarker 2.0 on ten datasets.

sections.heading: Question
sections.body: Can a general-purpose large language model replace the manual step of matching each cluster's highly expressed genes to known marker genes?

sections.heading: Approach
sections.body: The authors built GPTCelltype, an R package that turns per-cluster gene lists into a prompt ('Identify cell types of <tissue> cells using the following markers…') and sends it to GPT-4 or GPT-3.5 through the OpenAI API. They tested basic, chain-of-thought and repeated (majority-of-five) prompts, and top 10/20/30 genes from Wilcoxon or t-tests.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.body: Ten datasets across five species and hundreds of tissue and cell types, including normal tissue (HuBMAP Azimuth, GTEx, Human and Mouse Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens) and cancer (B-cell lymphoma, lung and colon cancer). Each prediction was mapped to Cell Ontology terms and scored 1 (full match), 0.5 (partial, same broad type) or 0 (mismatch) against the original authors' manual labels. Simulations tested mixed cell types, unknown cell types, missing genes and noisy gene lists.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: GPT-4 fully or partially matched manual labels for over 75% of cell types in most studies and tissues, and did best with literature-derived markers and with the top ten Wilcoxon genes; prompt strategy made little difference. It was strongest on immune cells and weaker on subtypes, very small clusters (≤10 cells) and B-lymphoma malignant cells. It separated pure from mixed types with 93% accuracy and known from unknown with 99%, and gave the same answer 85% of the time on repeated queries. API cost stayed under $0.10 for all queries in the study.

key_findings: Top 10 differential genes from a two-sided Wilcoxon test is the best input
Outperformed SingleR, ScType and CellMarker 2.0 on average agreement score
Some 'mismatches' were GPT-4 being more specific than the manual label (e.g. fibroblast vs. stromal cell)
Major types are matched more often than fine subtypes such as CD4 memory T cells
limitations: Training data are undisclosed, so the basis for an annotation can't be checked; the authors recommend expert validation
Risk of hallucination; noisy or unreliable differential genes degrade results
Datasets published before GPT-4's September 2021 training cutoff may have been seen in training
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (algorithm, preferred). This is the baseline the project's agent has to beat: an LLM annotating clusters from marker lists, with a reusable scoring scheme (Cell Ontology full/partial/mismatch) we can adopt for our own benchmarks.

sequencing.summary: Reuses published datasets; no new sequencing.

quantification.summary: Count matrices taken from the original studies.

preprocessing.summary: Library-size normalization and log1p transform of raw counts; differential genes per cell type with Seurat FindAllMarkers (Wilcoxon or t-test, logFC ≥ 0.25, detected in ≥10% of cells).

dimensionality_reduction.summary: Not part of the method; it starts from cluster-level gene lists.

batch_correction.summary: Some source datasets were batch-corrected by their original authors (e.g. ComBat for GTEx); not performed here.

clustering.summary: Uses the original authors' clusters / manual cell type groups as given.

annotation.summary: GPT-4 is prompted with each cluster's top differential or marker genes and the tissue name, and returns one cell type per cluster; results are scored against manual labels via Cell Ontology terms.
methods: LLM prompting with marker gene lists

papers.title: Fully-automated and ultra-fast cell-type identification using specific marker combinations from single-cell transcriptomic data
papers.reason: scType: marker-combination annotation algorithm with positive and negative markers
papers.why_listed: scType: positive/negative marker rules; ships marker DB; immune-heavy

sources.label: Europe PMC full text (results, discussion, methods, data and code availability)

ingestion.notes: The marker database itself (sctype.app) was not downloaded; marker examples below are only those stated in the text.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: ScType annotates clusters automatically from a large curated database of positive and negative markers, weighting each marker by how specific it is to one cell type; it labeled 72 of 73 cell types correctly across six datasets and runs far faster than comparable tools.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Manual marker-based annotation is slow and error-prone because markers are shared across cell types (e.g. CD44 across many immune cells), negative markers are rarely used, and reference-based classifiers need a well-matched reference.

sections.heading: The ScType database
sections.body: Built by merging CellMarker and PanglaoDB after harmonizing gene symbols and removing weakly supported markers (one supporting reference in CellMarker, or seen in fewer than five clusters in PanglaoDB). It includes negative markers from the literature, and users can add their own.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Within a tissue, each marker gets a specificity score: 1 for a marker listed for only one cell type, falling toward 0 as it's listed for more. Expression is z-scored per gene and multiplied by specificity; a cell type's score per cell is the sum over its positive markers minus the sum over its negative markers. Scores are summed per cluster and the top cell type wins. Clusters whose best score is negative or below a quarter of the cell count are labeled 'unknown'.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: On six human and mouse datasets (liver, pancreas, PBMC, brain, mouse lung and retina) it labeled 72 of 73 cell types correctly, including 8 that the original authors had labeled wrongly or too broadly. It matched or beat scSorter, SCINA and scCATCH on accuracy in 5 of 6 datasets and was over 30× faster than scSorter. In simulations it stayed above 90% accuracy at 80% dropout and flagged held-out unknown types in 43 of 45 datasets.

sections.heading: Cancer extension
sections.body: An optional module calls SNVs in COSMIC cancer genes from scRNA-seq reads and runs CopyKAT for aneuploidy, then labels a cluster non-malignant if its SNV score is under 20 and most cells are diploid. Demonstrated on an AML patient sample.

key_findings: Negative markers fix close calls: adding CCR7 and SELL as negative markers for effector T cells let it separate naive from effector/memory T cells in PBMCs

sources.label: Europe PMC full text (results, discussion, methods, data and code availability)

ingestion.notes: Supplementary notes and data files were not read.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: A multi-agent LLM system that annotates clusters, checks itself, scores its own confidence and explains its reasoning; across 970 cell types it beat existing methods by 12–41% in fully correct annotations, and it does notably well on cancer cells and fine T cell states.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Single-prompt LLM annotation (e.g. GPTCelltype) can hallucinate, gives every answer with the same confidence, doesn't explain itself, and uses few markers, so it struggles with subpopulations.

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.body: Five core agents: an Annotator (zero-shot chain-of-thought, mimicking an expert's workflow), a Validator that checks marker–cell type consistency and sends failures back to the Annotator, a Formatter, a Quality Scorer (0–100), and a Reporter that writes a full reasoning report. Optional agents: Annotation Boost (re-examines low-scoring calls using the full FindAllMarkers table), Subclustering (annotates all subclusters of one population together), Consensus Similarity (agreement across repeated runs) and a RAG agent (CellMarker 2.0 markers plus Cell Ontology trees).

sections.heading: Inputs
sections.body: Species, tissue, and per-cluster markers, typically from Seurat FindAllMarkers or Scanpy rank_genes_groups. The top 50 markers worked best; accuracy plateaus after that. Clustering is done beforehand by the user.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: On GTEx, Tabula Sapiens, Human Cell Landscape, Mouse Cell Atlas and Azimuth it raised fully correct annotations by 12–41% and fully-or-partially correct by 9–20% over the next-best method. In cancer data it found 72.5% of cancer cells (vs. 20% for GPTCelltype), rising to 88–100% with one extra prompt line, and it recognized brain metastases from lung primaries. On PBMC68k and the ProjecTILs T cell reference it improved accuracy by 27% and was the only method that consistently separated naive, memory and exhausted T cells.

sections.heading: Confidence and error-checking
sections.body: Quality scores below 75 mostly flagged wrong or partial calls; scores above 90 were mostly correct. Annotation Boost fixed 24 of 27 low-scoring wrong calls without breaking correct ones. High-confidence disagreements also exposed likely errors in gold-standard labels (e.g. 'monocytes' that express Schwann cell markers).

key_findings: Self-validation plus a confidence score lets users tell low-quality annotations from good ones
Works across underlying models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.92, GPT-4o 0.88, LLaMA-3.2-90B 0.82 on a 100-cell-type benchmark
Detects mixed clusters (90% in 50:50 simulations) and cancer cells far better than single-prompt LLMs
About $0.02 per annotation with GPT-4o; ~2 minutes for 20 clusters on 8 cores
limitations: Depends on marker quality; weaker on continuous developmental data (0.53 average accuracy on a mouse organogenesis atlas)
Clustering must be done externally
Results vary with the underlying commercial LLM and its version
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (algorithm, preferred). The most complete published agent design for annotation, and directly relevant to the group's focus: it was tested on cancer cells and on fine T cell states from the ProjecTILs reference. Its validator, quality score and boost agents are patterns our agent can reuse.

preprocessing.summary: Seurat v5 NormalizeData, then FindAllMarkers (min.pct 0.1, adjusted p < 0.05, log2FC > 0.25) to get per-cluster markers; the authors recommend QC, doublet detection and ambient RNA correction first.

clustering.summary: Assumes clustering is done externally; an optional Subclustering agent annotates subclusters of one population together. Future versions may integrate clustering.

annotation.summary: Multi-agent LLM annotation with validation loop, quality scoring, reasoning reports, optional boost, consensus and RAG agents; evaluated with Cell Ontology full/partial/incorrect scoring.
methods: RAG over CellMarker 2.0 and Cell Ontology

papers.title: Interpretation of T cell states from single-cell transcriptomics data using reference atlases
papers.reason: ProjecTILs: T cell reference atlas plus projection algorithm

sources.label: Europe PMC full text (results, methods, data and code availability)

ingestion.notes: The perturbation and infection results sections were skimmed. Markers are listed as given in the paper; the reference is murine (mouse gene case), and human data are projected via orthologs.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: ProjecTILs projects new T cell scRNA-seq data onto a fixed, annotated reference atlas of tumor-infiltrating T cell states without distorting it, labels each cell by nearest neighbors (91.6% correct in cross-validation), and flags query cells that deviate from known states.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: T cell subtypes and states are defined inconsistently across studies, so results from different datasets, diseases and species are hard to compare.

sections.heading: Reference atlases
sections.body: A murine TIL atlas of 16,803 T cells from 25 samples across six studies (melanoma and colon adenocarcinoma tumors plus tumor-draining lymph nodes), integrated with STACAS. It has nine states: CD8 naive-like, early-activation, effector-memory, precursor-exhausted (Tpex) and terminally exhausted (Tex); CD4 naive-like, Th1-like, Tfh and Treg. A second atlas covers virus-specific CD8 T cells in acute and chronic LCMV infection.

sections.heading: Projection algorithm
sections.body: The query is log-normalized, non-T cells are removed with TILPRED, and the query is batch-aligned to the reference with STACAS/Seurat anchors. The reference's own PCA rotation and UMAP model are then applied to the query, so the reference map never changes. A nearest-neighbor majority vote in PCA or UMAP space assigns each query cell a state. ICA components and discriminant genes reveal programs where the query deviates from the reference.

sections.heading: Validation
sections.body: In leave-samples-out cross-validation, 90% of projected cells landed within one UMAP unit of their true position and 91.6% got the right state. Tumor-specific OVA-tetramer+ CD8 T cells projected mostly to Tex (90.2%), as expected.

sections.heading: Human tumors
sections.body: Human TILs from melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, breast, liver, lung and colorectal cohorts, projected through mouse orthologs, showed the same subtypes in both species. Expanded, tumor-specific clones sat in Tex, Tpex and part of the effector-memory compartment, supporting a model in which EM cells give rise to Tpex and then Tex.

key_findings: Reference projection keeps the annotated map stable, so different studies can be compared on the same coordinates
T cell subtypes in tumors are conserved across cohorts, cancer types and between human and mouse
Tpex vs. Tex is defined by TCF7/IL7R/XCL1-high, low-cytotoxicity Tpex versus GZMB/PRF1-high, HAVCR2-high proliferating Tex
limitations: Reference atlases are murine; human data go through ortholog mapping
Covers T cells only; other cell types must be filtered out first
Cells in states absent from the reference can only be flagged as deviating, not named
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (algorithm, preferred). A reference-projection method built specifically for T cells in tumors, one of the group's two focus lineages, with explicit marker definitions for each T cell state. CASSIA also uses its T cell reference as a hard benchmark for fine T cell states.

dimensionality_reduction.summary: The reference's PCA rotation and UMAP model are applied to the query so it lands in the unchanged reference space; ICA (50 components) is used to find gene programs where the query deviates.

batch_correction.summary: STACAS (anchor-based, built on Seurat) integrates studies to build the atlases and aligns each query to the reference before projection.

clustering.summary: SNN clustering of the integrated reference, then manual annotation of clusters into functional states.

annotation.summary: Nearest-neighbor majority vote against the annotated reference assigns each query cell one of nine T cell states; reference states were defined by marker expression, expression gradients and MAST enrichment. Compared with Azimuth, scmap and SingleR.

trajectory.summary: TCR clonal sharing is used to infer a differentiation path (effector-memory → Tpex → Tex), but no trajectory algorithm is run.

papers.why_listed: LLM + database verification (CZ CELLxGENE) to curb hallucination

ingestion.notes: Read the full v1 preprint. Exact accuracy numbers are only shown in figures, which weren't readable from the PDF text, so results are described qualitatively.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: An LLM proposes the top 3 candidate cell types from a cluster's marker genes, then CZ CELLxGENE expression data picks the final label, which beats both LLM-only (GPTCelltype) and database-only annotation and reduces hallucination.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: LLMs like GPT-4 annotate clusters well from marker genes but can hallucinate, and nothing grounds their answer in real expression data.

sections.heading: Method: two stages
sections.body: Stage 1: an LLM is prompted with the tissue and marker genes and returns its three most likely cell types, in order. Stage 2: for each candidate, the agent looks up how strongly and how widely the marker genes are expressed in that cell type in CZ CELLxGENE Discover (for the given species and tissue, or across tissues if the tissue is unknown). A selection score adds the LLM's rank to the expression-based ranks, and the highest-scoring candidate wins.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.body: Nine datasets (303 cell types from 36 tissues), reusing the GPTCelltype benchmark: Human and Mouse Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, HuBMAP Azimuth, GTEx, CNS B-cell lymphoma, colorectal and lung cancer. Scored with GPTCelltype's Cell Ontology agreement score, and compared with GPTCelltype, CELLxGENE alone and PanglaoDB.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: CellTypeAgent beat every comparison method on all nine datasets. Stronger base models (best: o1-preview) gave better results, and the gain over LLM-only annotation was largest with weaker models. With the open-source DeepSeek-R1 it improved by 5.1%, which matters where data privacy rules out closed models. CELLxGENE alone often couldn't separate similar types (e.g. pericytes vs. mural cells); the LLM step narrows the choices first.

sections.heading: What didn't help
sections.body: Adding literature snippets (LitSense) or NCBI gene summaries to the prompt made results worse: the LLM over-relied on the pasted text, prompts got costlier, and many papers report markers only in figures or supplements.

key_findings: Verification against a real expression database reduces hallucination and improves accuracy
Using the top 3 LLM candidates worked slightly better than other candidate counts
More marker genes generally improved annotation
Can flag mixed populations when told a sample might be a mixture
limitations: Short preprint (not peer-reviewed in this version); figure-level numbers not given in text
Depends on the cell types and tissues present in CELLxGENE
Takes marker gene lists as input; clustering and marker selection happen upstream
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rule 3 (algorithm, preferred) and Dr. Talkington's own 'useful' example. It's the closest design to our project: an agent that combines LLM reasoning with database verification. The finding that pasting literature into prompts hurts accuracy is directly relevant to how our agent should use the ingested papers.

annotation.summary: Two-stage agent: LLM proposes ranked top-3 candidates, then CELLxGENE scaled expression and expressed-fraction of the markers re-rank them; the top-scoring candidate is the label. Optional literature and gene-summary tools were tested and rejected.

sources.label: Europe PMC full text (results, methods, data availability)

ingestion.notes: Kinetics and clonotype sections were skimmed. All markers are mouse genes.

enhanced_abstract.tldr: A reference map of ~35,000 virus-specific mouse CD4 T cells from acute and chronic LCMV infection, defining six major states (Th1 and Tfh effector and memory, central memory and its precursor) that can be used with ProjecTILs to label CD4 T cells in other datasets.

sections.heading: Goal
sections.body: Give CD4 T cell states a consistent definition and track how they change over the course of acute versus chronic viral infection.

sections.heading: Data and map
sections.body: Virus-specific (GP66:I-Ab+) CD4 T cells sorted at several timepoints after acute (Armstrong) or chronic (Clone 13) LCMV infection: 11 samples, 35,488 cells after QC, some with paired TCR sequencing. Integrated with STACAS, clustered with Seurat and annotated by canonical markers into six major states plus three minor ones (including Tregs).

sections.heading: Biology
sections.body: In acute infection cells shift from effector to memory states, with subtype-specific gene modules and timing; in chronic infection they take on distinct chronicity programs. Clonal responses were private to each mouse, and most clones produced both Tfh and Th1 cells regardless of TCR.

sections.heading: Use as a reference
sections.body: Datasets from other studies, tissues and perturbations were projected onto the map with ProjecTILs after purifying CD4 T cells with scGate. Tumor-specific CD4 T cells from a colon carcinoma model mostly matched Tfh (in lymph nodes) and Th1 effector or Treg states (in tumors), but the tumor 'Th1' cells formed a separate cluster with Th2-like genes (Ccl1, Ccr8, Il13), showing how the tools flag states the reference doesn't contain.

key_findings: Six major CD4 states defined by explicit marker combinations
Tcm and Tcm-precursor cells are defined mainly by lacking Th1/Tfh programs and sharing Ccr7, Klf2, S1pr1
Practical toolkit for detecting novel states after projection (radar plots, re-embedding, discriminant genes, silhouette scores)
limitations: Mouse viral infection, not human cancer
Focused on one lineage (virus-specific CD4 T cells)
Tumor CD4 T cells only partly match the viral reference
enhanced_abstract.why_it_matters: Rated 'later' (rule 1 exception: a reusable reference map, but set in viral infection) and Dr. Talkington's example of a less useful paper. It defines CD4 T cell states with clear markers, which could help refine T cell annotation later; it isn't needed for the initial build.

sequencing.summary: Sorted antigen-specific CD4 T cells on 10x Chromium (5′ or 3′), some samples hashtagged with TotalSeq antibodies, with paired TCR sequencing; Illumina NextSeq/NovaSeq.

quantification.summary: Count matrices from Cell Ranger; TCRs merged with scRepertoire.

preprocessing.summary: QC: >700 genes, 1,500–15,000 UMIs, <50% ribosomal, <10% mitochondrial, plus per-sample outlier removal; UCell signatures to remove contaminating cell types; scGate to purify CD4 T cells in external data.

dimensionality_reduction.summary: 20 dimensions for integration; UMAP of the reference space; query projection reuses reference embeddings.

batch_correction.summary: STACAS integration of 11 samples (800 variable genes excluding mitochondrial, ribosomal, heat-shock, interferon, cell-cycle and TCR genes).

clustering.summary: Seurat FindNeighbors/FindClusters (k = 10, resolution 0.4), then clusters merged and annotated into nine functional clusters.

annotation.summary: Clusters annotated by canonical markers and differential expression; the resulting map is a reference for ProjecTILs label transfer, with tools to detect states not in the reference.

trajectory.summary: Effector-to-memory transitions are inferred from timepoints and TCR clonal sharing, not from a trajectory algorithm.
